gist: Bankless's weekly roll-up covers the failed BIP 110 fork — the anti-ordinals Bitcoin purist chain that launched on 8 August with 2.53% of hash power against a 55% target and died because its proponents never adjusted difficulty — which Nick Carter is calling the death of Bitcoin maximalism. The market section centres on Michael Saylor's third consecutive week of selling (1,691 BTC for $650m of dollar reserves, below his ~$75k cost basis) against Bitcoin holding just under its rising 200-week moving average, gold up 14% since 17 July on PBOC liquidity, and Robinhood Chain taking the number-one Ethereum L2 revenue slot at $3.6m in July, 38% of all L2 revenue.

insights.claim: Michael Saylor's Strategy sold 1,691 bitcoin over the past week to add $650 million to its USD reserve — the third consecutive week of meaningful selling — taking dollar-denominated yield coverage to 2.7 years.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: The largest structural bid in Bitcoin has become a persistent seller; the number to track is weekly clip size, because consistency of selling matters more to price than total amount.

insights.claim: Saylor is selling below his roughly $75,000 average cost basis to defend STRC — now trading above 95 and approaching par — meaning he has prioritized the credit vehicle's health over accumulating Bitcoin at depressed prices.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Confirms the preferred-stock structure now constrains Strategy's Bitcoin behavior — the credit instrument is the tail wagging the dog, which changes how to model Strategy's future bid.

insights.claim: Both Bitcoin and Ether ETFs have been net buyers across June, July and August so far, effectively absorbing Saylor's sales — the hosts frame it as Saylor handing coins to BlackRock.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Persistent ETF absorption is why a multi-week seller of size has produced only a 2.5% weekly decline — the marginal buyer has changed hands from corporate treasury to ETF flows.

insights.claim: The hosts split on whether Saylor is the suppressing factor: Hoffman thinks the slow drip keeps price down and a faster capitulation would let Bitcoin reawaken, while Adams argues the disorderly-unwind risk is now on the back burner and Saylor is no longer the main character.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman and Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Frames the key question for Bitcoin's bottom: whether the overhang clears through a violent flush or a slow burn that suppresses price for months.
insights.quote: It's not a violent vomiting. It's more like a kind of a a burp, you know, like a a steady burp of Bitcoin coming off the balance sheet.

insights.claim: Adams contrasts Saylor with Tom Lee, whose ETH vehicle has bought roughly $25 million of ETH every week for about a year, has sold none, holds no credit instrument and sits just under 5% ownership — a cleaner balance sheet with no forced-seller mechanism.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: The structural difference between leveraged and unlevered treasury vehicles is now visible in behavior — a reason ETH's treasury bid is more durable than Bitcoin's in this drawdown.

themes.theme: Cycle positioning and the gold rotation

insights.claim: Bitcoin fell about 2.5% on the week to roughly $63,300, sitting just below a 200-week moving average around $63-64,000 that is itself creeping upward — it was $61,500 at the capitulation low when Bitcoin fell from $75,000 to $59,000.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A rising 200-week MA means time is working against sideways price — the level that was support at $61.5k now sits above spot, defining the line that decides the cycle read.

insights.claim: Hoffman argues this is fair value but not deep value: historically deep-value entries sit 5-10%+ below the 200-week moving average, and this cycle has only been briefly and shallowly below it.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable entry rule: wait for 5-10% below the 200-week MA (roughly high $50ks here) for a deep-value add rather than buying the fingernail dip.

insights.claim: Hoffman has moved from roughly 60% confidence that Bitcoin has already bottomed two weeks ago to about 40% now, turning moderately more bearish and planning to buy only if a new low prints.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A tracked sentiment shift from a well-followed crypto commentator — useful as a contrarian gauge of how thoroughly capitulated the informed retail cohort is.

insights.claim: The hosts cite Michael Nadeau's view that the bear cycle is 85% complete with a bottom due within two months (making it a 12-month bear), and Ben Cowen's call for an October bottom followed by up-only.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Two independent cycle analysts converging on an October-ish bottom gives a dated window to test the four-year-cycle thesis that most of crypto has been questioning.

insights.claim: Gold is up 14% since 17 July with futures around $4,500, clearing that level for the first time since 5 June — after peaking near $5,500-5,600 an ounce in late January and bottoming just below $4,000, having started January 2024 at $2,000 and January 2025 at $2,600.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams and David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Gold's move from $2,000 to $5,600 and back to $4,500 is the reference series for the debasement trade — Bitcoin's failure to follow is the anomaly demanding explanation.

insights.claim: The hosts attribute gold's renewed strength to Michael Howell's global liquidity work: the PBOC is back injecting liquidity after a pause from roughly February-March, and because crypto is banned, capital controls bind and property has burned Chinese savers, that liquidity flows into gold.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Gives a monitorable driver for gold — PBOC liquidity injections — and explains why this leg of the debasement trade has not been shared with Bitcoin.

insights.claim: The Bitcoin/gold ratio has fallen 69% this cycle versus 82% in the 2018 bear and 75% in 2022, and appears to have bottomed and turned up — the hosts' argument that gold strength is dry tinder for Bitcoin rather than competition for it.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: The ratio bottoming is the cleanest cross-asset signal offered: if it holds, Bitcoin outperforms gold from here even if both rise on the same liquidity impulse.

insights.claim: Howell's framework holds that PBOC liquidity props up gold specifically while Fed and rest-of-world liquidity is what drives crypto assets — so the current gold move is not yet the signal for Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Gives a specific trigger to watch for the Bitcoin turn — Fed and G4 liquidity expansion rather than the Chinese impulse currently lifting gold.

insights.claim: CPI came in at 3.4%, up 0.1% month-on-month and in line with analyst expectations, with the S&P and Nasdaq slightly higher on the news.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: An in-line 3.4% print keeps the liquidity path unchanged — no forcing event either way for the Fed-liquidity trigger the Bitcoin thesis depends on.

themes.theme: The BIP 110 fork that died in two blocks

insights.claim: Bitcoin forked on Saturday 8 August at block 961,632 when nodes enforcing the BIP 110 soft fork rejected an Antpool block for lacking the required signal — the culmination of a months-planned split by the anti-ordinals, anti-arbitrary-data camp.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: The first real test of Bitcoin's consensus mechanism since 2017 — and its outcome sets the precedent for how future contentious changes resolve.

insights.claim: The fork attracted 2.53% of hash power against a 55% target and its proponents never adjusted the difficulty parameter, so blocks that should have taken 10 minutes would have taken close to a year — killing the chain immediately.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A technical own-goal that removes any near-term risk of a purist chain fragmenting Bitcoin — and demonstrates how thin the maximalist faction's actual resources are.

insights.claim: No exchange listed the forked asset and no meaningful miner support materialized, so the split never reached the threshold at which the usual legitimacy sequence — node adoption, exchange listing, market price, then miner migration — can even be tested.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Lays out the actual legitimacy pipeline for any future fork — a checklist for judging whether a contentious chain split is a real risk or theater.

insights.claim: Hoffman's answer to who decides what Bitcoin is: the market, in the aggregate of node operators, miners, exchanges and ETF issuers — and ultimately price, as demonstrated when Bitcoin Cash came within about 15% of flipping Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A working model of protocol governance: price is the arbiter, so any fork's threat level is a function of what a market will pay for it, not its technical merits.

insights.claim: Nick Carter is calling this the death of Bitcoin maximalism, citing hardcore foot soldiers defecting to a doomed ultra-orthodox faction plus purist influencers exposed by the Coldcard hardware wallet hack and a purist merchant payment service hack.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: The ideological constituency that historically blocked Bitcoin protocol change has visibly weakened — raising the probability of future Bitcoin functionality expansion that maximalists once vetoed.

insights.claim: Adams notes the composition of Bitcoin decision-makers has changed since 2017 — Michael Saylor was not a participant in the block size wars and now is, while hardcore maximalist influencers have become more muted.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Institutional and treasury holders have displaced ideological node-runners as the marginal governance power in Bitcoin — a structural change in how the asset evolves.

themes.theme: Robinhood Chain and the L2 revenue league

insights.claim: Robinhood Chain became the number-one Ethereum L2 by blockchain revenue in its first full month live, generating $3.6 million in July — 38% of all L2 revenue.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A brokerage-owned chain taking 38% of L2 revenue in month one shows distribution beats technology in the rollup market — bearish for L2s whose only edge is technical.

insights.claim: Robinhood Chain has app-layer TVL just shy of $1 billion across Morpho, Uniswap and others, plus over $1 billion of stablecoin supply — but the strategically important metric, stock-token TVL, is only $30 million despite tripling from $10 million.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: The tokenized-equity thesis is not what is driving Robinhood Chain's revenue — memecoin trading is, which is the reason to doubt the revenue's durability.

insights.claim: Base has fallen to third among L2s by revenue, behind Polygon proof-of-stake, which the hosts find surprising given Polygon's activity beyond Polymarket and stablecoins.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: A meaningful ranking change in the L2 landscape — Coinbase's chain losing the revenue crown to two chains with different distribution models.

insights.claim: A Sprite Hood NFT mint on Robinhood Chain by Cole, the original creator of Pudgy Penguins, sold 37,000 NFTs at $17 and 5,000 more at $117 for about $1.3 million total.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Right-sized NFT economics — $1.3m rather than hundreds of millions — is what a genuine sector recovery would look like early; the hosts put NFT comeback odds in the teens.

insights.claim: The FOMO trading app added roughly 40,000 new signups in a month generating 400,000-500,000 trades, monetizing swaps directly and taking user relationships — and therefore revenue — out of Pump's pocket, sparking an open fight over user acquisition.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: The value migration to the consumer front-end is the recurring pattern in crypto: Pump verticalized to capture Raydium's fees and is now being disintermediated at the app layer itself.

insights.claim: Adams notes memecoins have persisted through the bear market — Pump still throws off significant revenue, FOMO is growing fast, and memecoin activity is what drives Robinhood Chain — which he reads as evidence they will feature in the next bull cycle rather than fading like NFTs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Bear-market durability is the strongest available evidence that memecoin infrastructure is a persistent revenue category, not a cycle artifact — relevant to valuing Pump-style cash flows.

insights.claim: Polymarket puts the Clarity Act at roughly 18% (as low as 15% this week) to pass this year despite a September vote being expected, because delay benefits both Democrats wanting to wait until after midterms and the banks.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Market-implied odds of US crypto market-structure legislation this year are now low — a repeated pattern of scheduled votes that slip, which argues against positioning for legislative catalysts.

insights.claim: The hosts identify a silver lining in Clarity failing: the bill's bank compromise would have closed the stablecoin yield loophole, so its failure preserves native yield on stablecoins for crypto users.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Reframes legislative failure as partially bullish for stablecoin issuers and DeFi yield products — the opposite of the consensus 'regulation good' framing.

insights.claim: Paul Atkins's SEC may deliver parts of the Clarity Act by regulation, potentially starting with a token safe harbor — but its durability depends on the 2028 election outcome.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Regulatory rather than legislative relief arrives faster but is reversible — a reason to discount rule-based clarity when underwriting long-dated crypto business models.

insights.claim: Fidelity is filing to stake up to 100% of its roughly $1 billion Ethereum ETF and pay holders quarterly cash distributions, setting up a direct experiment against BlackRock's version where staking yield accrues in the underlying.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: A clean natural experiment on whether investors pay up for cash distributions versus NAV accrual — the answer will shape ETF product design across staking assets.

insights.claim: The EIP to cap ETH staking issuance is effectively dead: Hoffman reports that people inside the Ethereum Foundation and its spin-offs will not spend social capital publicly arguing the pro side, which he reads as recognition of a losing cause.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Removes a live tail risk to the ETH yield narrative just as staking ETFs launch — the two stories are directly connected even though the hosts hoped they weren't.

insights.claim: Adams argues cutting ETH issuance would destroy the very feature Wall Street prefers about ETH versus Bitcoin — a yielding internet bond — with annualized ETH issuance already under about 0.8%, at or below Bitcoin's and well below gold's.
insights.speaker: Ryan Sean Adams
insights.so_what: Positions ETH's yield as its institutional product-market fit rather than a monetary flaw — with a 1-3% yield 'Goldilocks zone' as the stated target range.

insights.claim: Venice's VVV token burn hit seven consecutive daily all-time highs, peaking at about $14,000 burned on 10 August against a prior equilibrium of $9-10,000 per day — with the token price falling as revenue rises.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman
insights.so_what: Rising revenue against a falling token price is the classic setup the hosts flag as mean-reverting — a specific small-cap to watch for the fundamentals-catch-up trade.
